market_context: United States/general English; fresh cod compared with dried salted and desalted cooked cod
title: Cod: protein, fat, salt, and nutrition

seo.title: Cod: protein, fat, salt, and nutrition
seo.meta_description: Fresh cod is lean and protein-rich; dried salted cod can exceed 7 g sodium per 100 g before desalting. Water loss and salt curing radically change the numbers.
seo.search_intent: Understand cod nutrition and why fresh, salted and desalted cod show very different protein, calorie and sodium values.

excerpt: Raw Atlantic cod is about 82 calories, 17.8 g protein and less than 1 g fat per 100 g. Dried salted cod concentrates protein and sodium as water is removed; desalting then changes the composition again.
content_html:
Cod is a very lean white fish, but nutrition tables can look contradictory because “cod” may mean fresh fish, dried salted fish, or cod that has already been soaked and cooked. Those forms cannot be compared per 100 g as if they contained the same amount of water.

Fresh cod: high protein, very little fat

A USDA reference for raw Atlantic cod provides about 82 calories, 17.8 g protein and 0.7 g fat per 100 g. It also contains about 54 mg sodium and 413 mg potassium.

Cooking removes water, concentrating protein by weight. Depending on method and doneness, cooked cod commonly lands around 20–23 g protein and roughly 90–105 calories per 100 g, with less than 1 g fat if no oil is added.

Salt cod is a different product by weight

During curing, cod loses substantial water and gains a large amount of salt. A dried salted cod reference reaches roughly 290 calories, 62.8 g protein and 7,027 mg sodium per 100 g.

That does not mean a prepared serving delivers three times as much protein as fresh cod. Drying removes water, so 100 g of the cured product contains far more fish solids. During desalting, the fish absorbs water again and sodium diffuses out.

Desalting can dramatically reduce sodium

One food-composition reference for desalted, cooked cod lists about 84 calories, 20.4 g protein, 0.25 g fat and 134 mg sodium per 100 g. That is dramatically lower sodium than the dried salted starting reference.

The final value depends on piece thickness, soak time, temperature, water changes and starting salt concentration, so there is no single universal sodium number for “desalted cod.”

How long does salt cod need soaking?

Thick loins generally require more time than small flakes. Home cooks commonly soak it under refrigeration and replace the water several times. The purpose is to create a concentration gradient that lets sodium diffuse out of the fish over time.

Cod remains a lean fish

At roughly 0.7 g fat per 100 g raw, cod is far leaner than salmon, which commonly provides around 10–13 g fat per 100 g depending on species and origin. Adding 15 g cooking oil contributes about 135 calories—much more energy than the cod's own fat.

Is cod a good protein source?

Yes. A 150 g cooked serving at about 21–22 g protein per 100 g provides roughly 31–33 g protein. With cured cod, the main nutrition variable to watch is not protein but how much sodium remains after desalting.

Bottom line

Fresh cod is lean and protein-rich; salt cod concentrates protein and especially sodium because water has been removed. Always check whether a nutrition value refers to fresh, dried salted, or desalted cod.

faq.question: How much protein is in cod?
faq.answer: Raw Atlantic cod is about 17.8 g per 100 g. Cooking can raise the concentration to roughly 20–23 g per 100 g as water is lost.

faq.question: Is cod high in salt?
faq.answer: Fresh cod is naturally low in sodium. Dried salted cod can exceed 7,000 mg sodium per 100 g before soaking.

faq.question: Does desalting remove all the salt?
faq.answer: No, but it can reduce sodium dramatically. The result depends on thickness, soak time and water changes.
